title: ekklesia
summary: The references portray a gathered people through several images and practices. Acts 2 describes a community devoted to teaching, shared meals, prayer, and care for one another. Ephesians 4 pictures a body whose members contribute to its growth; 1 Peter 2 describes a people and spiritual household; Hebrews 10 urges believers to keep meeting and encourage one another. The texts illuminate communal identity and life, but not every reference uses the same term or image.
historical_context: The set includes a narrative snapshot in Acts and instruction in Ephesians, 1 Peter, and Hebrews. These contexts describe early Christian communities as the texts present them; the sources do not support a broader reconstruction of how all ancient associations or assemblies functioned.
canonical_context: Acts emphasizes shared teaching, meals, prayer, and generosity. Ephesians uses the body image to describe unity and contribution; 1 Peter uses household and peoplehood language; Hebrews stresses gathering and mutual encouragement. Together these passages show community as both shared identity and practice, with different authors using different descriptions.
literary_context: Acts narrates communal life, while the letters exhort and teach their readers. Ephesians develops a body metaphor, 1 Peter draws on household and people imagery, and Hebrews gives a direct appeal to continue meeting. The forms help readers distinguish a narrated scene from a metaphor or instruction.
covenantal_significance: The passages connect belonging with practices that sustain a community: learning, worship, care, mutual contribution, and encouragement. They give a fuller picture of shared life than a definition based only on a gathering or institution.
canonical_role: This entry brings together biblical portrayals of Christian assembly and community. Its references connect a narrated gathering with later instruction and metaphors for shared identity, while preserving the terms each passage uses.

interpretive_notes.note: Do not reduce ekklesia to a single English gloss.
Check the immediate context and genre before drawing theological conclusions.
